title: Your first pattern
summary: Why regular expressions are everywhere at work, literal text, the twelve special characters, and escaping safely in C#.

steps.title: A pattern describes text
body: A **regular expression** (regex) is a small pattern that describes text. You will use them every week:
- **Search**: find every log line with a request id, every call to a method across a repository.
- **Validate**: is this a ticket key, a date, a version number?
- **Extract**: pull the status code and duration out of an access log.
- **Refactor**: rename `GetUser(` to `GetUserAsync(` in 300 files with one find-and-replace.
The simplest pattern is plain text. `timeout` matches the letters t-i-m-e-o-u-t, in that order, anywhere in a line.
It is case-sensitive by default: `Timeout` is a different text.
Below, the pattern runs for real in .NET. Change it to `Timeout`, or press the **i** flag to ignore case.

steps.prompt: The pattern `error` runs over these four lines. Which lines contain a match?
steps.explain: Matching is case-sensitive, and a match can sit inside a longer word: `errors` contains `error`. Lines 1 and 4 have the wrong capital letters.

steps.title: Twelve characters are special
body: These characters do not match themselves. They are the regex language:
```text
The one that bites most often is the dot: `.` matches **any single character**. So `1.5` matches `1.5`, but also
`105` and `1x5`. To match a special character itself, put a backslash before it: `1\.5` matches only `1.5`.
Why it matters: a search for the IP `10.0.0.1` without escaping also finds `10a0b0c1` and `1000001` in a log.
Usually harmless in a search, a real bug in a firewall rule or a validator.

steps.title: Find version 1.2, and only 1.2
prompt: Release notes mention many versions. Write a pattern that finds the text `v1.2` and nothing that only looks like it.
It must find `v1.2` in `release v1.2 ships` but find nothing in `v1x2`, `v102` or `v1.3`.
hints: `v1.2` almost works. Which part of it is special?
Escape the dot: `\.` matches a real dot.
steps.explain: `v1\.2`: the backslash turns the dot back into a plain dot. Without it, `v1.2` also matches `v1x2` and `v102`.

steps.prompt: Outside square brackets, which characters must you escape with `\` to match them literally?
steps.explain: The special twelve are `. * + ? ^ $ ( ) [ ] { } | \`. A dash is only special inside `[ ]`, and `#` only in `x` (IgnorePatternWhitespace) mode.

steps.title: Regex in C#: verbatim strings and Regex.Escape
body: In C#, `System.Text.RegularExpressions.Regex` runs patterns. Write patterns in **verbatim strings** `@"..."`, so
a backslash stays one backslash. In a normal string, `"\d"` is a compile error and `"\\d"` is hard to read.
```csharp fragment
using System.Text.RegularExpressions;
bool found = Regex.IsMatch(line, @"v1\.2");     // true if there is a match anywhere
When part of the pattern comes from a user or a config file, **escape it** with `Regex.Escape`. Otherwise a search
for `a.b` matches `axb`, and a search for `(` throws an exception. That is a real bug and a small security hole:
users can make your pattern do things you did not intend.
```csharp fragment
string term = "api.contoso.com";
bool mentions = Regex.IsMatch(line, Regex.Escape(term));   // pattern: api\.contoso\.com

steps.explain: An unescaped dot matches the `7` in `3750`. Escaped, it only matches a real dot.

steps.prompt: Complete the code: does the log line mention the host the user typed?
steps.explain: `Regex.IsMatch` answers yes or no. `Regex.Escape` makes the user's text literal.

steps.title: A Windows path, literally
prompt: Find the folder `C:\Temp\logs` in a line of a deployment script. A backslash is special in a regex, so it needs
Find it in `copy *.log C:\Temp\logs now`, but not in `C:/Temp/logs` or `C:\Temp\log`.
hints: A literal backslash is written `\\` in the pattern.
steps.explain: `C:\\Temp\\logs`: each `\\` is one literal backslash. In C# you would write `@"C:\\Temp\\logs"`, or let `Regex.Escape` do it.

steps.title: Does this line mention the host?
prompt: Write `bool MentionsHost(string line, string host)`. It returns true when `line` contains `host` exactly as written.
Host names contain dots, so escape the host before using it as a pattern. Use `Regex.IsMatch`.
template: Dojo.Eq("api.contoso.com is in the GET line", true, MentionsHost("GET api.contoso.com 200", "api.contoso.com"));
Dojo.Eq("apixcontoso.com is not api.contoso.com", false, MentionsHost("GET apixcontoso.com 200", "api.contoso.com"));
Dojo.Eq("10.0.0.1 is in the deny line", true, MentionsHost("deny 10.0.0.1:22", "10.0.0.1"));
Dojo.Eq("a host with ( does not crash", false, MentionsHost("GET svc 200", "svc(1)"));
hints: Build the pattern from the host with `Regex.Escape(host)`.
